task_brief: Day 2 of "Algorithms, Efficiency, and Correctness" (unit 2, grade 10) is a worked-model trace on sorting algorithms. It is one step inside the unit — not the whole unit project — and takes about 45–75 minutes. The unit is working toward: Compare searching and sorting approaches using complexity reasoning together with measured runtime evidence. Today's work contributes to that by handling sorting algorithms at the explicit model stage, against the unit's wider topics of searching algorithms, sorting algorithms, recursion and base cases, and complexity and growth rates. This session is formative: it is scored on completeness and honesty of the record, not on getting a polished result.
primary_task: Work through the complete central input printed in activity_setup for sorting algorithms, one step at a time rather than reading it straight through. For each step, write what changed and why that step is legal. Build a trace table with one row per step showing the values or states before and after. Then change exactly one line, value, or condition in the model, predict the new result before running or re-tracing it, and record whether your prediction was right. Explain in your own words the rule that makes sorting algorithms behave the way the model shows. The activity_setup block below supplies the complete central input, exact specification, execution method, test cases, debugging target, and equal-credit manual simulation; use those exact materials rather than waiting for another handout, account, service, or tool. Anchor today's work inside its unit: this session's evidence is about sorting algorithms, and it belongs to "Algorithms, Efficiency, and Correctness", which also covers separate topics such as searching algorithms. Close out with this check before you stop: Explain the modelled approach to sorting algorithms in your own words and name the step most likely to go wrong. At grade 10 the bar is independent work that justifies its approach against a named alternative you considered and rejected, with the trade-off stated concretely.

central_input.title: Inline sorting algorithms code case
central_input.purpose: Use this exact fictional case to investigate sorting algorithms; no other file, model, dataset, or account is needed.

expected_behavior_and_specification: The algorithm must return the greatest member of a nonempty list; the supplied list must return 7.
The invariant is that best equals the greatest value examined so far, including when every value is negative.
The submitted explanation must connect the observed control flow or data state to sorting algorithms, not merely state the final number.
The boundary test must be completed and its actual result compared explicitly with the expected result.

execution_method.primary: No-install browser method: open any browser developer console, paste the complete starter code, press Enter, and record the output or exact error text.
execution_method.local_optional: If Node.js is already installed, save the unchanged snippet as activity.js and run `node activity.js`; installing Node.js is not required.
execution_method.no_computer_required: The hand-trace route below is a complete execution method and earns identical credit.

debugging_target.observed_failure: Starting best at 0 violates the stated invariant for an all-negative list, so the second test incorrectly returns 0.
debugging_target.target: Choose an initialization supported by the nonempty-list specification, state the loop invariant, and rerun all three tests.
debugging_target.passing_change: Initializing best from values[0] makes the invariant true before iteration; the tests return 7, -2, and 6.
debugging_target.scope_note: Diagnosing the state, control-flow, or data defect and connecting the repair to sorting algorithms is the central evidence.

equal_credit_alternative.method: Paper or notes-app simulation; this earns exactly the same score as running code.
steps: Make one row for each statement or loop check and copy the starting input exactly.
Record every variable, object field, selected item, and output after that step.
Circle the first row where the actual state stops matching the specification.
Apply the one repair named in your explanation and trace all three tests again.
equal_credit_alternative.evidence_to_submit: The completed trace, the one-line corrected condition, and an expected-versus-actual table for all three tests.

test_or_check_criteria: The trace table has one row per step and shows values or states both before and after that step.
Every step carries a written reason that step is legal, not just a restatement of what happened.
Exactly one deliberate change was made to the model, with a prediction recorded before the re-run and the outcome after.
The rule governing sorting algorithms is restated in the student's own words rather than copied from the model.

presentation_and_privacy.sandbox_and_credentials_note: Everything in this task runs in a sandbox or on paper. Never use a real password, passphrase, API key, account credential, access token, precise home location, or any real person's identifiable information — invent fictional values instead. Do not sign into, probe, scan, stress, or attempt access to any live, production, school, or third-party system, and do not bypass a filter, licence, access control, or terms of service. Any practice login used in an example must be obviously invented — a silly made-up name paired with a nonsense multi-word phrase — and must never be anything you or anyone in your family actually uses somewhere real. If a task seems to need something real, substitute a made-up stand-in and note the substitution.

copyright_and_authorship: The graded submission must be your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI tool may explain an idea, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but must not produce, write, debug, or make any part of the work that is scored. Any code, asset, or text you did not write must be openly licensed or supplied for this task, and must be cited in a comment or note naming where it came from and what you changed.

remediation: Reteaching for sorting algorithms follows the signal actually observed, not a fixed script. If the signal is "prerequisite gap": Return to the smallest prerequisite needed for sorting algorithms, model it in a concrete or text-only representation, then retry one fresh item. If the signal is "procedure without understanding": Ask the learner to explain or represent why the approach to sorting algorithms works before continuing. If the signal is "correct but low confidence": Confirm the reasoning specifically, offer one varied example of sorting algorithms, and avoid unnecessary remediation. If the signal is "repeated error pattern": Name the observable pattern neutrally, contrast it with a worked example, and schedule a short same-day or next-session review. If the signal is "requests the answer to graded work": Explain the concept, ask a diagnostic question, or help isolate the defect. Do not supply the graded artifact, solution code, or finished creative work. If the signal is "mastery evidence": Require accurate independent application plus explanation on a later or different occasion before marking sorting algorithms mastered. Re-check with one fresh item of the same kind before moving on, and record which signal was seen so the pattern is visible across the unit rather than treated as a one-off.
extension: Apply sorting algorithms under a new constraint, compare two approaches or perspectives, or explain the idea to someone else using an original example. Treat this as optional depth on sorting algorithms rather than extra volume: one harder case done well beats three more of the same. Extension work stays inside the same sandbox rules — no real credentials and no live external systems. Extension work is never required to reach mastery and must not be assigned as a penalty.
